subtopics.title: Geography and Basic Facts
subtopics.summary: The Aravalli range is the oldest mountain system in India, about 2 billion years old and dating to the Precambrian era. It extends 692 km from Champaner in Gujarat through Rajasthan and Haryana to Delhi. Its highest peak is Guru Shikhar, at 1722 m, near Mount Abu in Rajasthan.
facts: Oldest mountain system in India, about 2 billion years old
Dates to the Precambrian era
Extends 692 km from Champaner (Gujarat) to Delhi
Passes through Gujarat, Rajasthan, Haryana and Delhi
Ends at Raisina Hill in Delhi
Highest peak: Guru Shikhar, 1722 m
Guru Shikhar is near Mount Abu in Rajasthan
Source of rivers including Luni, Banas and Sabarmati
Mineral base: copper, zinc, lead, silver and Makrana marble
Boasts 22 wildlife sanctuaries, four tiger reserves and bird parks

subtopics.title: Ecological Services of the Range
subtopics.summary: The range works as a natural barrier that slows the eastward spread of the Thar Desert by blocking dust-laden desert winds. It deflects moisture-laden monsoon winds eastward, shields northern plains from cold, dry winter winds from Central Asia, and filters pollution for Delhi-NCR. Its fractured, weathered rocks let rainwater infiltrate and recharge aquifers in semi-arid regions.
facts: Natural Great Green Wall: barrier against eastward spread of the Thar Desert
Blocks dust-laden desert winds
Monsoon modulator: deflects moisture-laden winds eastward toward the Indo-Gangetic Plains
Aids rainfall distribution in North India
Winter climate shield against cold, dry winds from Central Asia
Forested stretches absorb carbon dioxide in Delhi-NCR
Forested stretches trap PM2.5 and improve air quality
Highly fractured and weathered rocks enable rainwater infiltration
Recharges aquifers in semi-arid Rajasthan, Haryana and Gujarat
Habitat for over 300 plant species and 120 bird and animal species

subtopics.title: Mining Curbs and the 2025 Supreme Court Ruling
subtopics.summary: Protection measures began with 1990s mining restrictions and continued through Supreme Court orders, including a 2009 blanket mining ban in parts of Haryana and a 2024 order barring fresh leases. In 2025 the Court accepted a uniform scientific definition of an Aravalli hill, based on an MoEF&CC expert committee. The Forest Survey of India assessment found that over 90 per cent of the Aravalli landscape would be excluded under the 100 m threshold, which sparked fears of more mining and construction.
facts: 1990s: restrictions on mining
2009: SC blanket mining ban in parts of Haryana
MC Mehta vs Union of India: mining restricted and banned across large parts of the range
2024: SC order bars fresh leases; Central Empowered Committee tasked with scientific review
2025 definition based on MoEF&CC Expert Committee
Aravalli hill: landform rising 100 m or more above its immediate local terrain
Aravalli ranges: clusters of such hills within 500 m, including intervening areas
Mining banned in core/inviolate areas such as protected areas, ESZs, wetlands and tiger reserves
Freeze on new mining leases until a Management Plan for Sustainable Mining is prepared by the Indian Council of Forestry Research and Education
Over 90% of Aravalli landscape excluded by the 100 m threshold

subtopics.title: Aravalli Green Wall and Afforestation Policies
subtopics.summary: The Aravalli Green Wall Project, inspired by Africa's Great Green Wall, is a 1400 km by 5 km ecological corridor across Gujarat, Rajasthan, Haryana and Delhi, launched in 2019. It targets restoring 1.1 million hectares by 2027 through native plantations, around 1,000 nurseries and removal of invasive species. Wider national policies include the National Forest Policy's one-third target, the National Mission for a Green India, CAMPA and India's Bonn Challenge pledge.
facts: 1400 km x 5 km ecological corridor across Gujarat, Rajasthan, Haryana and Delhi
Covers 29 districts
Target: restore 1.1 million hectares by 2027
Launched in 2019; nodal ministry is the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change
Works: native plantations, around 1,000 nurseries, invasive species removal, water body restoration
National Forest Policy (1988): at least one-third of land under forest/tree cover
National Mission for a Green India is part of the National Action Plan on Climate Change
CAMPA uses funds collected from diverted forest land for afforestation
Bonn Challenge: India aims to restore 26 million hectares by 2030
Matri Van Initiative: 750-acre urban forest under 'Ek Ped Maa Ke Naam'

subtopics.title: Why MGNREGA Is Being Replaced
subtopics.summary: The Viksit Bharat G RAM G Bill 2025 was introduced in the Lok Sabha to replace MGNREGA, which was enacted in 2005. The government argues that the older framework is outdated given changes in the rural economy, livelihoods and employment patterns. Criticism of the older scheme includes the creation of low-utility or non-durable assets and a funding model that is open-ended.
facts: Bill name: Viksit Bharat - Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) Bill, 2025
Introduced in Lok Sabha to replace MGNREGA
MGNREGA was enacted in 2005
Framework argued to be outdated given changes in rural economy, livelihoods and employment
Criticism over creation of low-utility or non-durable assets
Shift from open-ended funding to normative allocations aims at better fiscal management
Farmers report labour shortages during sowing and harvest seasons
Bill is framed under the national vision of Viksit Bharat @2047

subtopics.title: Key Features of the Bill
subtopics.summary: The bill raises the statutory work guarantee to 125 days per rural household per financial year and lets states suspend the scheme for up to 60 days in sowing and harvesting seasons. Works must align with four national priorities for durable asset creation. An unemployment allowance applies if work is not provided within 15 days of a household's application.
facts: 125 days of guaranteed unskilled manual work per rural household per financial year
Earlier guarantee under MGNREGA was 100 days
States can suspend the scheme for up to 60 days during sowing and harvesting seasons
Shift to a Centrally Sponsored Scheme with shared financial responsibility
States/UTs funding: 60% Centre : 40% State
North-Eastern and Himalayan States funding: 90% Centre : 10% State
Four priorities: Water Security, Core Rural Infrastructure, Livelihood-related Infrastructure, Special Works for Extreme Weather Events
Unemployment allowance if work is not provided within 15 days of application
Weekly wage payments are envisaged

subtopics.title: MGNREGA vs the Proposed Bill
subtopics.summary: The comparison sets out the two frameworks on guaranteed workdays, wage funding, nature of the right, budgeting, operating period and payment timing. MGNREGA gave a justiciable right with open-ended funding, while the proposed bill makes the guarantee subject to a fixed budget cap. The bill also allows seasonal pauses and envisages weekly wage payments.
facts: Guaranteed workdays: MGNREGA at least 100 days; proposed bill 125 days
Wage funding: MGNREGA Centre bears 100% of unskilled wage cost; proposed 60:40 for most states
Nature of right: MGNREGA is justiciable, citizens can sue if work is denied; proposed is a schematic entitlement
Budget cap: the proposed guarantee is limited by a fixed budget cap
Budgeting: MGNREGA uses a labour budget reflecting actual demand; proposed uses a fixed state-wise allocation
Operating period: MGNREGA runs continuously; proposed allows suspension for up to 60 days in peak seasons
Payment frequency: MGNREGA mandates payment within 15 days of work completion; proposed envisages weekly payments

subtopics.title: Planning, Oversight and Related Schemes
subtopics.summary: Gram Panchayats prepare Viksit Gram Panchayat Plans, which are integrated with PM Gati Shakti and aggregated through VB-NRIS for national planning. Panchayats are graded on development indicators, and councils and steering committees oversee implementation. Several other rural schemes address livelihoods, skilling, property cards and traditional artisans.
facts: Viksit Gram Panchayat Plans (VGPPs) are prepared by Gram Panchayats
VGPPs are integrated with PM Gati Shakti for infrastructure convergence
Plans are aggregated through Viksit Bharat National Rural Infrastructure Stack (VB-NRIS)
Panchayats are graded on development indicators; underperforming ones get higher allocations
Central and State Gramin Rozgar Guarantee Councils review, monitor and advise
National and State Steering Committees make recommendations on allocation and convergence
Digital ecosystem with biometric authentication and AI analytics to reduce leakages
SVAMITVA gives property cards; PM Vishwakarma supports artisans via skilling, toolkits and credit

subtopics.title: Lok Adalat: Concept and Features
subtopics.summary: A Lok Adalat, whose name means 'People's Court', settles cases pending in court or at the pre-litigation stage through compromise. It is based on Gandhian principles and offers an expeditious, cost-effective alternative to dispute resolution. Lok Adalats have statutory status, and every award they make is final and binding on all parties.
facts: Lok Adalat means 'People's Court'
Based on Gandhian principles
Covers cases pending in court and pre-litigation disputes
Disputes are compromised or settled in an amicable manner
First Lok Adalat in India organised in Gujarat in 1982
Statutory status under the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987
Usually a judicial officer as Chairman, with a lawyer and a social worker as Members
Non-compoundable offences fall outside its purview
Every award is final and binding on all parties
Organising authority: National Legal Services Authority

subtopics.title: Types: National and Permanent Lok Adalats
subtopics.summary: The National Lok Adalat is held at regular intervals across India on a single day, and since 2015 it has been held on a specific matter every month. The Permanent Lok Adalat was created by a 2002 amendment to handle disputes involving public utility services. The Supreme Court has described a Lok Adalat as purely conciliatory.
facts: National Lok Adalat: held across India on a single day
Since 2015, held on a specific matter every month
Permanent Lok Adalat introduced by a 2002 amendment to the 1987 Act
Handles public utility services such as transportation and telegraph
Chaired by a District Judge or Additional District Judge, or one who held higher judicial office
Two other persons with adequate experience in public utility services sit on it
No jurisdiction over offences not punishable by law
Its judgments are final and binding on all parties
State of Punjab vs Jalour Singh (2008): Lok Adalat is purely conciliatory

subtopics.title: NALSA and Legal Aid Institutions
subtopics.summary: The Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 was enacted to build a nationwide network for free and competent legal services, and it came into force on 9 November 1995. The National Legal Services Authority (NALSA) was founded in 1995 under the Act. Legal aid institutions operate at national, state, district, taluka and High Court and Supreme Court levels, and Article 39A provides for free legal aid.
facts: 1980: a national-level committee named CILAS was set up to supervise legal aid programmes
Legal Services Authorities Act enacted in 1987
The Act came into force on 9 November 1995
Aim: nationwide network for free legal services to weaker sections
NALSA founded in 1995 under the 1987 Act
Article 39A provides free legal aid to poor and weaker sections
Chief Justice of India is Patron-in-Chief of NALSA
Institution levels: national, state, district, taluka/sub-division, High Court, Supreme Court
High Court committee headed by the Chief Justice of the State High Court
Objectives include free legal aid, legal awareness, Lok Adalats and compensation to crime victims

subtopics.title: e-Courts Project and Digital Tools
subtopics.summary: The e-Courts Project brings Information and Communication Technology into Indian courts, with Phase I running in 2007-2015 and Phase III from 2023 onwards. The National Judicial Data Grid is an online database of orders, judgments and case details created under Phase II. SUVAS, FASTER and SUPACE help with translation, secure transmission of orders and access to laws for judges.
facts: e-Courts Project: ICT enablement of courts
Phase I implemented during 2007-2015
Phase II started in 2015
Phase III spans four years, from 2023 onwards
Funded by the Department of Justice, Ministry of Law and Justice
National Judicial Data Grid: database of orders, judgments and case details, developed by the National Informatics Centre
SUVAS: Supreme Court Vidhik Anuvaad Software, an AI-trained translation tool
FASTER: Fast and Secured Transmission of Electronic Records
SUPACE: Supreme Court Portal for Assistance in Court's Efficiency
Swapnil Tripathi v Supreme Court of India (2018): live streaming is part of the Article 21 right to access justice
Gujarat High Court is the first court to live stream judicial proceedings on its YouTube channel

subtopics.title: Key features of the Assam Bill
subtopics.summary: The Assam Assembly passed the Prohibition of Polygamy Bill 2025 to eliminate polygamous practices, with strict penalties. It applies to Assam residents and to certain people in polygamous marriages outside the state, while excluding Scheduled Tribes and Sixth Schedule areas. It holds village heads, qazis, parents and legal guardians accountable and creates a State Victim Relief Fund.
facts: Assam Assembly passed the Prohibition of Polygamy Bill 2025.
Objective: eliminate polygamous practices, with strict penalties.
Applies to residents of Assam.
Also covers individuals in polygamous marriages outside Assam or availing Assam's welfare schemes.
Excludes Scheduled Tribes under Article 342 and Sixth Schedule areas of Assam.
Grandfather Clause validates pre-law marriages compliant with personal or customary laws.
Village heads, qazis, parents and legal guardians are held accountable for polygamous marriages.
State Victim Relief Fund compensates women affected by polygamous marriages.
Convicted individuals are barred from government jobs, benefits, schemes and electoral participation.
Imprisonment of up to 10 years for entering a second marriage while the first is still legally valid.

subtopics.title: Polygamy: meaning, types and status
subtopics.summary: Polygamy is a marital system in which one person has more than one spouse at the same time. Polygyny means one man with several wives, and polyandry means one woman with several husbands. NFHS-5 (2019-21) puts the national rate at 1.4 per cent, with Meghalaya highest at 6.1 per cent and Assam at 2.4 per cent.
facts: Polygamy: a marital system with more than one spouse at the same time.
Polygyny: one man has multiple wives.
Polyandry: one woman has multiple husbands.
National polygamy rate in India is 1.4 per cent (NFHS-5, 2019-21).
National rates by religion: Hindus 1.3%, Muslims 1.9%, Christians 2.1%, Sikhs 0.5%, Others 2.5%.
Meghalaya has the highest rate in India at 6.1 per cent.
Assam's rate is 2.4 per cent: Hindus 1.8%, Muslims 3.6%.
NFHS-5 measures the share of currently married women (age 15 to 49) whose husband has other wives besides themselves.

subtopics.title: Personal laws and marriage legislation
subtopics.summary: Marriage law in India varies across personal laws. The Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 prohibits bigamy for Hindus, while the Muslim Personal Law (Shariat) Application Act, 1937 permits polygamy. The Special Marriage Act, 1954 allows inter-religious marriages but explicitly prohibits polygamy, and the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 makes marrying again during a spouse's lifetime an offence.
facts: Hindu Marriage Act, 1955: bigamy is prohibited for Hindus.
Contracting a second marriage while the first subsists is a punishable offence under the Hindu Marriage Act.
Muslim Personal Law (Shariat) Application Act, 1937: polygamy is permitted.
Marriages under the Shariat Act that violate Fundamental Rights can be legally challenged.
Special Marriage Act, 1954: allows inter-religious marriages while explicitly prohibiting polygamy.
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023, Section 82: offence of marrying again during the lifetime of a spouse.
Punishment under Section 82 of the BNS: up to 7 years' imprisonment along with a fine.

subtopics.title: Uniform Civil Code and judicial background
subtopics.summary: A Uniform Civil Code (UCC) would give all citizens one common set of personal laws, irrespective of religion. Article 44 places the duty to implement it on the state, though the Directive Principles are not enforceable. The 2018 Law Commission report judged a UCC neither necessary nor desirable at this stage, while the Supreme Court has repeatedly called for uniformity in personal laws.
facts: UCC: a common set of personal laws for all citizens irrespective of religious affiliation.
Article 44 of the Directive Principles sets out the duty of the state to implement a UCC.
Directive Principles are not enforceable.
Personal laws were placed in the Concurrent List, allowing both Parliament and State Assemblies to legislate.
The framers of the Constitution did not intend total uniformity in personal laws.
Law Commission (2018): reform and codify family laws across religions; a UCC is neither necessary nor desirable at this stage.
Shah Bano case (Mohd Ahmed Khan vs Shah Bano Begum, 1985): highlighted the need for uniformity in personal laws.
Sarla Mudgal vs Union of India (1995): highlighted the need for reforms in personal laws.
Shayara Bano vs Union of India (2017): held talaq-e-biddat (triple talaq) unconstitutional.
Supreme Court hailed Goa as a 'shining example' of a functioning UCC.

topics.title: Indian Rupee Breaches 90 per US Dollar in 2025

subtopics.title: The 90 per Dollar Breach
subtopics.summary: In 2025 the Indian rupee crossed 90 per US dollar after depreciating over 5% during the year, even though India had strong 8.2% GDP growth and low inflation. The 90 level carries psychological weight, since crossing it can activate buy-stop orders and intensify downward momentum. The booklet says the breach reflects cumulative pressures built over time rather than a single event.
facts: Rupee depreciated over 5% in 2025, crossing 90 per USD
India had strong 8.2% GDP growth and low inflation at the time
The 90 per USD level is psychologically important for traders
Crossing 90 can activate buy-stop orders
Buy-stop orders can intensify downward momentum
The breach reflects cumulative pressures, not a single disruptive event
Policymakers and investors watch global conditions, trade and domestic indicators

subtopics.title: Depreciation vs Devaluation
subtopics.summary: Rupee depreciation means the currency's value falls against foreign currencies, driven by market forces, capital flows, external shocks or policy uncertainty. Devaluation is different: the government or RBI deliberately reduces the currency's value, and it happens under fixed or pegged exchange rates. Depreciation happens under floating or managed-floating systems.
facts: Depreciation: the currency's value falls relative to foreign currencies
Causes of depreciation: market forces, capital flows, external shocks, policy uncertainty
Devaluation: government or RBI deliberately reduces the currency's value
Devaluation happens under fixed or pegged exchange rate systems
Depreciation happens under floating or managed-floating systems
Devaluation is a policy tool to boost exports and reduce deficit
Depreciation is driven by FPI outflows, inflation, CAD and global shocks

subtopics.title: Causes of Rupee Weakness in 2025
subtopics.summary: Analysts linked the rupee's weakness to a strong US dollar, uncertainty over the India-US trade deal and steep US tariffs on Indian exports. Foreign portfolio investors withdrew funds, while a wider trade deficit and speculative dollar demand added pressure in the forex market.
facts: Strong US dollar and delays in the initial tranche of the India-US trade deal
US tariffs of up to 50% reduced the competitiveness of Indian exports
Lower investor confidence reduced inflows
FPIs withdrew funds aggressively, causing capital outflows
Global uncertainty shifted capital to US Treasuries and USD as safe haven
Imports of gold, electronics, crude and machinery widened the trade deficit
Higher crude oil prices worsened the import bill
Importers front-loaded purchases, anticipating further rupee weakness

subtopics.title: Impacts of Rupee Depreciation
subtopics.summary: A weaker rupee makes Indian goods cheaper abroad, raises the value of remittances and can encourage domestic manufacturing. The booklet also lists costs: dollar-denominated debt becomes dearer, deficits widen, imported inflation rises, subsidy bills grow and consumer purchasing power falls. It also notes a capital flight risk when investor confidence weakens.
facts: Boost to exports: Indian goods become cheaper globally
Higher remittance value: NRIs get a more favourable exchange rate
Push to domestic manufacturing as expensive imports encourage local production
Costlier external debt for companies with dollar-denominated loans
Wider current account and trade deficits as imports become costlier
Higher subsidy burden as fertiliser imports become costlier
Imported inflation: crude, fertilisers and electronics become costlier
Capital flight risk as a weak rupee reduces investor confidence
Lower consumer purchasing power due to costlier essential imports

subtopics.title: Measures to Stabilise the Rupee
subtopics.summary: The booklet lists measures to stabilise the rupee, beginning with rupee-based trade settlement through Special Vostro Rupee Accounts. Other steps include offshore rupee trading, currency swaps, strong forex reserves with calibrated RBI intervention, and wider UPI internationalisation. It also proposes reducing gold imports through gold monetisation and digital gold.
facts: Increase Special Vostro Rupee Accounts for rupee-based trade settlement
Promote local currency settlement agreements with Asia, Africa and the Gulf
Promote offshore rupee trading
Push for inclusion of Indian G-Secs in global bond indices
Expand currency swap agreements and maintain strong forex reserves
Calibrated RBI intervention, including selling or buying USD
Expand UPI internationalisation and work towards INR eligibility for the IMF SDR basket
Reduce gold imports via gold monetisation and digital gold

topics.title: RBI Cuts Repo Rate to 5.25%: The Goldilocks Phase

subtopics.title: Dec 2025 Repo Rate Cut and Goldilocks Phase
subtopics.summary: In December 2025 the RBI cut the repo rate by 25 basis points to 5.25%, its fourth reduction in 2025. The RBI said the cut aims to sustain a Goldilocks phase of strong growth and low inflation. Inflation had fallen below the lower tolerance band, giving the central bank room to ease while growth stayed robust.
facts: RBI cut the repo rate by 25 basis points to 5.25% in December 2025.
The December 2025 cut was the 4th reduction by RBI in 2025.
Total reduction by RBI in 2025 was 125 basis points.
Goldilocks phase means not too hot (high inflation) and not too cold (low growth).
Goldilocks phase enables balanced and sustainable expansion.
GDP growth was 8.2% in Q2 FY2025-26.
Inflation was 1.7% in Q2 and dipped to 0.3% in October 2025.
Inflation fell below the 2% lower tolerance band of the RBI framework.
Reasons for cut: sustained disinflation, strong growth momentum, external risks.

subtopics.title: Repo Rate Transmission and Other Instruments
subtopics.summary: The repo rate is the rate at which RBI lends to commercial banks, and it moves borrowing costs across the economy. RBI raises it to curb spending when inflation is high and lowers it to pump money in during a liquidity crunch. Other tools include the reverse repo rate, Bank Rate, MSF, CRR, SLR and open market operations.
facts: Repo stands for 'Repurchasing Option' or 'Repurchase Agreement'.
Repo rate is the rate at which RBI lends money to commercial banks.
Reverse repo rate is the rate at which RBI borrows money from commercial banks.
In high inflation, RBI increases the repo rate to reduce the flow of money.
A higher repo rate makes loans costlier for banks and borrowing costly for businesses.
In a short-term liquidity crunch, RBI lowers the repo rate to pump funds into the economy.
Bank Rate is a long-term rate at which the central bank lends to other banks.
MSF is a window for banks to borrow overnight funds at a higher rate than the repo rate.
CRR is the proportion of deposits banks must hold as cash with RBI.
SLR is the minimum share of deposits banks must hold as liquid cash, gold or other securities.
Open market operations: purchase or sale of government securities to inject or absorb liquidity.

subtopics.title: Monetary Policy Committee and Inflation Targeting
subtopics.summary: The MPC is a statutory body that sets the benchmark policy rate needed to contain inflation within the target range. It has six members, the RBI Governor chairs it ex officio, and decisions are taken by majority vote with the Governor holding a casting vote in a tie. India's flexible inflation targeting uses a 4% target with a 2% tolerance band, formalised by the Urjit Patel Committee (2014).
facts: The MPC is a statutory body under the RBI Act, 1934.
The Central Government is empowered to constitute a six-member MPC.
MPC members: RBI Governor, Deputy Governor in charge of monetary policy, one RBI officer nominated by the central board, and three members appointed by the Central Government.
The RBI Governor is the ex-officio chairperson of the MPC.
The MPC must meet at least four times a year.
Quorum is four members, including the RBI Governor or, in his absence, the Deputy Governor.
Decisions are by majority vote; the Governor has a casting vote in a tie.
MPC decisions are binding on banks.
Inflation target is 4% with a 2% band (2% to 6%).
India adopted flexible inflation targeting in 2016.
Urjit Patel Committee (2014) formalised inflation targeting; the target was first proposed by the Chakravarty Committee (1982-85).
The inflation target is set by the government in consultation with RBI every 5 years.
RBI releases a Monetary Policy Report every six months, forecasting inflation 6-18 months ahead.

subtopics.title: Inflation Measures: CPI, WPI and GDP Deflator
subtopics.summary: Inflation is an increase in the overall prices of goods and services in an economy over time, and it is tracked through several indices. CPI measures retail inflation and covers both goods and services, while WPI covers only goods and reflects wholesale prices. The GDP deflator compares annual production value at current prices with a base year.
facts: Inflation is an increase in the overall prices of goods and services in an economy over time.
CPI measures inflation in the retail market.
CPI has a base year of 2012.
CPI is released by the National Statistical Office (NSO).
CPI includes both goods and services.
CPI reflects up-to-date expenditure patterns.
WPI includes only goods and does not consider the services sector.
WPI is released by the Office of Economic Advisor, Ministry of Commerce and Industry.
GDP deflator compares annual production value at current prices to a base year.

subtopics.title: RBI: Origins and Core Functions
subtopics.summary: The RBI is the central bank responsible for managing India's financial system. It was established on April 1 in Calcutta, was later nationalised from private stakeholders, and performs supervisory, monetary, currency and banking roles. Its concept was inspired by Dr. Ambedkar's strategies in his book on the rupee.
facts: RBI is the central bank responsible for managing the country's financial system.
RBI's concept was inspired by Dr. Ambedkar's strategies in his book 'The Problem of the Rupee'.
RBI was established on April 1 in Calcutta.
RBI was nationalised; it was previously owned by private stakeholders.
Supervisory function: issue bank licences, open branches, set minimum reserves and inspect commercial banks.
Monetary authority: maintain price stability while promoting economic growth.
Issuer of currency: exchanges and destroys currency notes.
Manager of foreign exchange and custodian of India's forex reserves.
Lender of last resort and banker to the government and to other banks.
Custodian of the cash reserves of commercial banks.
Regulates the forex market through exchange rules.

subtopics.title: Economic, Energy and Payments Cooperation
subtopics.summary: The 23rd annual summit adopted Programme 2030 to diversify India-Russia ties beyond defence and energy. The programme sets a trade target of $100 billion by 2030, against $68.7 billion recorded in 2024-25. Cooperation also covers national-currency settlements, payment-system interoperability and continued support for nuclear energy projects.
facts: Programme 2030 adopted to diversify ties beyond defence and energy.
Coordinated by the India-Russia Inter-Governmental Commission on Trade, Economic, Scientific, Technical and Cultural Cooperation (IRIGC-TEC).
IRIGC-TEC is chaired by India's External Affairs Minister and Russia's Deputy Prime Minister.
Trade target: $100 billion by 2030.
Trade stood at $68.7 billion in 2024-25.
Settlements in national currencies to be boosted.
Work on interoperability of payment systems and CBDCs to bypass Western financial systems (SWIFT).
Negotiations on an FTA with the Eurasian Economic Union to be fast-tracked.
Continued support for Kudankulam Nuclear Power Plant, Small Modular Reactors and future civil nuclear projects.

subtopics.title: Defence and Strategic Cooperation
subtopics.summary: India and Russia focus on joint R&D, co-production under Make in India, military technology transfer and regular exercises. The RELOS agreement provides mutual logistics support for troops, warships and aircraft during operations away from home bases. The 2+2 Ministerial Dialogue aligns foreign and defence ministers on strategic priorities.
facts: RELOS: Reciprocal Exchange of Logistics Agreement, enabling mutual logistics support for troops, warships and aircraft.
RELOS scope: access to each other's military facilities, ports and airspace.
RELOS includes simplified refuelling and maintenance support for deployments.
Russia was India's main supplier of defence equipment (36%).
India-Russia 2+2 Ministerial Dialogue aligns Foreign and Defence Ministers.
Joint exercise: INDRA.
BrahMos: cruise missile jointly developed by DRDO and NPO Mashinostroyeniya (NPOM).
S-400 Triumf: long-range surface-to-air missile system procured by India.
Su-30MKI multi-role fighters produced in India by Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL).

subtopics.title: Connectivity and Logistics Corridors
subtopics.summary: The proposed Chennai-Vladivostok Maritime Corridor aims to cut transport time to Russia by 40 per cent and saves 3,028 nautical miles over the existing route. The International North-South Transport Corridor (INSTC) is a multi-modal route set up in 2000 by Iran, Russia and India. India-Russia Far East and Arctic cooperation is guided by a 2024-2029 programme.
facts: Chennai-Vladivostok Maritime Corridor is a proposed sea route passing through the Sea of Japan, South China Sea and Malacca Strait.
Aim: reduce transportation time to Russia by 40%.
Time saving: up to 16 days.
Distance saving: 3,028 nautical miles.
INSTC: multi-modal transportation route established in 2000 in St Petersburg by Iran, Russia and India.
INSTC aim: promote transportation cooperation among member states.
India-Russia Far East Cooperation Programme covers 2024-2029.
Key Far East and Arctic areas: agriculture and mining, manpower and pharmaceuticals, diamonds and shipping.
India is an Observer in the Arctic Council.

subtopics.title: Diplomacy, Counter-Terrorism and Honours
subtopics.summary: India and Russia signed a Treaty of Peace and Friendship in 1971 and a new Treaty of Friendship and Cooperation in 1993 after the Soviet Union dissolved. Both sides denounced the 2025 Pahalgam and 2024 Crocus City Hall attacks and called for strict action against UN-listed terrorist organisations. PM Modi was conferred Russia's Highest National Award, the Order of St Andrew the Apostle.
facts: Treaty of Peace and Friendship signed in 1971.
New Treaty of Friendship and Cooperation signed in 1993, after the dissolution of the Soviet Union.
PM Modi was conferred Russia's Highest National Award, the Order of St. Andrew the Apostle.
Order of St Andrew established by Tsar Peter the Great in 1698, reinstated in 1998 and abolished in 1918.
Ganga-Volga Dialogue: platform to enhance Special and Privileged Strategic Partnership; organised by the Ministry of External Affairs with Dr Syama Prasad Mookerjee Research Foundation.
Counter-terrorism: Pahalgam attack (2025) and Crocus City Hall attack (2024) denounced.
Both parties called for a Zero-Tolerance Policy and finalisation of the Comprehensive Convention on International Terrorism.
Russia formally joined the International Big Cat Alliance.
Russia reiterated support for India's permanent membership of a reformed and expanded UN Security Council.

subtopics.title: International Relations and Trade
subtopics.summary: This group covers the Durand Line, the 2,600 km boundary between Pakistan and Afghanistan that was fixed by a British-era agreement and has been contested since Partition. It also covers India's trade agreements with New Zealand and Oman expand trade and investment, with zero-duty access stated only for New Zealand. The section closes with the US National Security Strategy, the Preah Vihear temple dispute, and India's re-election to the IMO Council.
facts: The Durand Line is a 2,600 km international boundary between Pakistan and Afghanistan.
It was drawn through the Durand Agreement of 1893 between Sir Henry Mortimer Durand and Emir Abdur Rahman Khan.
Afghanistan refused to formally recognise the Durand Line, viewing it as a colonial imposition.
Treaty of Gandamak (1879) granted Britain control over Afghanistan's foreign affairs.
Treaty of Rawalpindi (1919) restored Afghanistan's foreign policy autonomy while reaffirming the Durand Line.
India-New Zealand FTA gives 100% of Indian exports to New Zealand zero-duty market access.
India-Oman CEPA is India's second CEPA in the GCC after the UAE and aims to expand trade beyond USD 10 billion.
US National Security Strategy reasserts the Monroe Doctrine (1823) and avoids branding Russia and China as existential threats.
ICJ (1962) gave sovereignty over Preah Vihear Temple to Cambodia; the 2013 ICJ clarification called for a demilitarised zone that was never fully implemented.
India was re-elected to the IMO Council's Category B for 2026-27 with the highest votes.

subtopics.title: Rights, Governance and Society
subtopics.summary: This group covers the Karbi Anglong unrest, where protests over land and resource rights under the Sixth Schedule have caused civilian deaths and internet shutdowns. It also covers the proposed Right to Disconnect, the Supreme Court's ruling on workplace harassment complaints under the PoSH framework, and Assam's proposal to grant ST status to six communities. The section ends with the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and Human Rights Day.
facts: Karbi Anglong unrest began with a hunger strike by indigenous tribal groups.
Protesters demanded eviction of long-settled non-tribal communities from protected grazing and tribal lands.
Karbi Anglong is administered by the Karbi Anglong Autonomous Council under the Sixth Schedule.
The Karbi Anglong Peace Accord 2021 was a tripartite agreement involving the Government of India, Assam and Karbi insurgent groups.
The Right to Disconnect would give employees a statutory right to refuse work calls, emails or messages beyond work hours and on holidays.
France's El Khomri Law (2017) was the first national law recognising the right to disconnect.
The Supreme Court (Sohail Malik case) held that women can approach the ICC at their own workplace over harassment by outsiders.
An Internal Complaints Committee is mandatory in every workplace employing 10 or more persons; a Local Committee applies where none exists.
Assam's Group of Ministers recommended ST status for 6 communities; ST (Plains) has 10% reservation and ST (Hills) has 5%.
The UDHR (1948) is not a legally binding treaty but forms the International Bill of Human Rights; Human Rights Day is observed on 10 December.

subtopics.title: Economy, Finance and Insurance
subtopics.summary: The RBI's National Strategy for Financial Inclusion 2025-30 sets out five pillars for widening access to financial services over the next five years. The section also explains masala bonds, which let Indian entities raise rupee-denominated debt overseas, and how taxes, cesses and surcharges differ in their use and sharing with states. Recent bills on a health-security cess and on insurance FDI complete the section.
facts: The National Strategy for Financial Inclusion 2025-30 was released by the RBI after approval by a Sub-Committee of the Financial Stability and Development Council.
The strategy defines 5 key pillars to guide India's financial inclusion roadmap for the next five years.
The pillars cover equitable access, gender-sensitive inclusion, linking livelihoods and skills, financial education, and customer protection.
The Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana (2014) enabled the opening of over 56 crore bank accounts.
Masala bonds are rupee-denominated debt issued in overseas markets; the IFC introduced them in 2014 on the London Stock Exchange.
The RBI governs masala bonds.
A cess is used only for its earmarked purpose, while a surcharge adds to Union revenue with no specific purpose.
Taxes are shared with states through the Divisible Pool.
The Health Security and National Security Cess Bill 2025 introduces a capacity-based excise cess; initial coverage includes Pan Masala.
The Sabka Bima Sabki Raksha (Amendment of Insurance Laws) Bill 2025 raises the FDI limit in Indian insurance companies from 74% to 100%.

subtopics.title: Environment, Energy and Disaster
subtopics.summary: India's updated seismic zonation map under the BIS 2025 Earthquake Design Code places the entire Himalayan arc in the new highest-risk Zone VI. The section also covers the SHANTI Bill 2025 for nuclear energy, CITES CoP20 and its appendix system, and UNEA-7, where India's wildfire resolution was adopted. The International Big Cat Alliance rounds out the wildlife items.
facts: The new Zone VI is the highest-risk zone and covers the entire Himalayan arc for the first time.
Towns located on boundaries between zones now automatically fall into the higher-risk zone.
75% of India's population lives in seismically active regions.
The National Center for Seismology operates the National Seismological Network and monitors earthquakes in real time.
The SHANTI Bill 2025 would replace the Atomic Energy Act 1962 and the Civil Liability for Nuclear Damage Act 2010.
CITES was signed on 3 March 1973 and came into force on 1 July 1975; CoP20 was held in Samarkand, Uzbekistan.
CITES Appendix I lists species threatened with extinction, where commercial trade is prohibited; Appendix II allows controlled trade.
UNEA-7 was held in Nairobi in 2025, and India's resolution on strengthening global wildfire management was adopted there.
Over 36% of India's forests are prone to frequent fires, according to the India State of Forest Report 2021.
The International Big Cat Alliance was launched in 2023 to celebrate 50 years of Project Tiger and aims to conserve 7 big cat species.

subtopics.title: History, Heritage and Health
subtopics.summary: This group traces Vande Mataram from its 1875 composition and the 1937 limit to two stanzas to its 1950 status as national song. It also covers Deepavali's 2025 UNESCO listing, the Goa Liberation Day commemoration, and the 25 December birth anniversaries of Vajpayee and Malaviya. The health item tracks India's HIV/AIDS response through NACP V and the 2024 figures.
facts: Vande Mataram was written in 1875 by Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay and was published in the 1882 novel Anandamath.
A 1937 Congress Working Committee decision limited national use of Vande Mataram to its first two stanzas.
On 24 January 1950, Dr Rajendra Prasad declared Vande Mataram the national song, to be honoured equally with the national anthem.
Unlike the national anthem, Vande Mataram is not enforceable under the Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act 1971.
Deepavali was added to UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage list in 2025; India's total entries now stand at 16.
Goa Liberation Day on 19 December commemorates Operation Vijay (1961), which ended 451 years of Portuguese rule.
Goa attained full statehood on 30 May 1987, becoming India's 25th state.
Atal Bihari Vajpayee (born 25 December 1924) and Pandit Madan Mohan Malaviya (born 25 December 1861) are honoured on their birth anniversaries, which mark Good Governance Day.
NACP V (2021-2026) is a central sector scheme aligned with SDG 3.3 to end AIDS as a public health threat by 2030.
HIV prevalence declined from 0.33% in 2010 to 0.20% in 2024, and new infections fell from 1.25 lakh to 64,500 over the same period.

Civil contempt: wilful disobedience of a judgment, decree, direction or order of a court

quizzes.title: Aravalli Range: Facts and Rulings
quizzes.passage: The Aravalli range is one of the oldest mountain systems in India. It runs through Gujarat, Rajasthan and Haryana, and reaches Delhi. The range acts as a natural barrier that slows the spread of the Thar Desert, because it blocks dust-laden desert winds. It also influences the southwest monsoon by guiding moisture-laden winds towards the Indo-Gangetic Plains. In winter, its hills shield the northern plains from cold, dry winds. Its forested stretches help clean the air of the National Capital Region by absorbing carbon dioxide and trapping fine particles. Its forests are also home to many plant and animal species. Rocks in the range allow rainwater to seep into the ground, which supports groundwater in semi-arid areas. The area also supports mining-based livelihoods and industries. Because of these uses, the range has faced pressure from mining and urban growth for many years. Courts and government bodies have therefore introduced several measures to limit mining and restore forests. In 2025, the Supreme Court accepted a uniform scientific definition of an Aravalli hill, based on an expert committee's advice. The definition determines which landforms receive protection, and it has raised concern that mining and construction could expand into areas left outside it. Understanding both the ecology and the legal steps helps explain why the range is in the news.

quizzes.title: Restoring the Green Cover
quizzes.passage: Restoring degraded land has become a central goal in the Aravalli region, where mining and urban growth have put pressure on the landscape for decades. Planners have drawn inspiration from a large African project that aims to hold back the spread of desert. The approach focuses on planting native species on degraded land to support ongoing afforestation. Nurseries are set up to grow saplings for continuing planting drives, so that seedlings are ready when they are needed. Damaged water bodies are also being restored. Invasive plant species are also removed. The work is coordinated centrally but depends on many partners, including non-governmental organisations, private companies and local communities. The National Forest Policy (1988) aims for at least one-third of total land area under forest or tree cover. The restoration is meant to control desertification, improve air quality and strengthen climate resilience in the Delhi-NCR region. Together, these measures aim to protect the region's green cover and water supply. The nurseries and planting drives span the states that the corridor crosses, including Haryana, Rajasthan, Gujarat and Delhi. Plantation work covers degraded land, and the approach relies on species that grow naturally in the region.

quizzes.title: Key features check
quizzes.passage:
Rural employment policy has been under review since the government introduced the Viksit Bharat - Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) Bill, 2025 in the Lok Sabha. The proposal would replace MGNREGA, which critics say has grown outdated as rural livelihoods and employment patterns have changed. Concerns have also been raised that the older scheme created assets of low utility or limited durability. The government presents the new law as part of its national vision of Viksit Bharat by 2047.

The funding model is also changing. The earlier scheme relied on open-ended funding that was largely borne by the Centre. The new bill moves to a model of shared financial responsibility between the Centre and the States, with different ratios for different regions. Supporters argue that predictable allocations make budgeting easier and help the Centre target spending.

Planning is meant to begin in villages. Gram panchayats prepare their own plans, which are linked to infrastructure programmes and then combined at the national level. Panchayats are also to be graded on development indicators. Oversight will come from councils at the Centre and in the States, along with steering committees that advise on allocations and coordination between ministries.

Farmers have long reported labour shortages during sowing and harvest seasons, and the bill gives States a tool to respond. Overall, the government says the reform will strengthen rural income security while improving transparency and accountability.

questions.q: What is the statutory guarantee of unskilled manual work per rural household per financial year under the proposed bill?
questions.explanation: The booklet states the bill guarantees 125 days per household per financial year, up from 100 days under MGNREGA.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): State governments can suspend the scheme for up to 60 days during sowing and harvesting seasons.
Reason (R): The suspension is meant to ensure availability of agricultural labour during these seasons.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.explanation: The booklet says the suspension is allowed to ensure availability of agricultural labour during sowing and harvesting seasons.

III. SVAMITVA   ->   C. Infrastructure convergence with village plans
IV. PM Vishwakarma   ->   D. Property cards to rural households

Consider the following statements about the VB-G RAM G Bill:
I. Panchayats that underperform on development indicators may receive higher allocations.
II. Works must align with five national priorities for durable asset creation.
III. Wages are envisaged to be paid weekly, instead of within a 15-day cycle.
Which of the above statements is/are correct?

quizzes.title: Planning and schemes check
quizzes.passage:
Rural employment policy is being reshaped to match changes in the countryside. A legal guarantee of work has long been the base of the framework, but critics have pointed to scattered works and to assets that did not last. The proposed replacement treats planning as a village-level exercise. Gram panchayats prepare plans for their areas, and those plans are meant to be linked with larger infrastructure programmes so that core rural infrastructure, water and livelihood works are coordinated rather than separate. The local plans are then combined into a national picture, which the government says will support coordinated planning across the country.

Beyond wage work, the government runs several rural programmes. One helps self-help groups build self-employment and access finance. Another aims to build skills among rural youth. A further programme gives rural households records of their property, and another supports traditional artisans with skilling, toolkits and credit. Together, these measures are presented as part of a wider effort to promote livelihoods in villages.

The bill also seeks tighter monitoring. Officials plan to use digital tools, including biometric checks and data analytics, to reduce leakages and track work. Social audits are to be strengthened so that local communities can review how public money is spent.

quizzes.title: Lok Adalat basics
quizzes.passage: Lok Adalat, whose name means 'People's Court', is a forum based on Gandhian principles that offers an expeditious and cost-effective alternative to dispute resolution through the courts. It works as a forum where cases that are pending in a court can be taken up, and disputes that are still at the pre-litigation stage can be brought before it as well. The aim is to have these matters compromised or settled in an amicable manner. A Lok Adalat organised for an area consists of serving or retired judicial officers and other persons of that area, as specified by the agency that organises it. In general, the panel has a judicial officer as Chairman, with a lawyer and a social worker as Members. Lok Adalats have been given statutory status by law, which places them firmly within India's legal framework. Every award made by a Lok Adalat is final and binding on all parties to the dispute. The organising authority for Lok Adalats is the National Legal Services Authority. Because the process rests on agreement between the parties, it saves time and money compared with a long trial. The panel's role is to help the parties arrive at a common outcome. The mechanism is therefore a key part of India's alternative dispute resolution system.

quizzes.title: Types of Lok Adalat
quizzes.passage: Lok Adalats take two main forms in the way they are organised. The National Lok Adalat is held at regular intervals across India on a single day, and in recent years it has also been held on a specific matter each month. The Permanent Lok Adalat is a different body, created to handle disputes involving public utility services such as transportation. Its chairperson is a District Judge or an Additional District Judge, or a person who is or has been a District Judge or has held a judicial office higher in rank. The chairperson sits with persons who have adequate experience in public utility services. A Permanent Lok Adalat has no jurisdiction over any situation involving an offence that is not punishable by law. Its judgments are final and binding on all parties involved. The Supreme Court has described a Lok Adalat as purely conciliatory, which means it works by helping the parties reach an agreement rather than by imposing a decision. Both forms aim to settle disputes quickly and at low cost, without the long process of litigation. Together, they show how the Lok Adalat system combines flexibility with binding outcomes, so that a settlement reached before the forum carries real legal weight.

quizzes.title: Assam Bill: practice MCQs
quizzes.passage: Polygamy is a marital system in which a person has more than one spouse at the same time. Its prevalence in India is measured through national family surveys, which ask married women about their husbands' marital arrangements and compare results across religions and states. Such data helps lawmakers judge whether a practice needs stronger legal action. In 2025 the Assam Assembly passed a Prohibition of Polygamy Bill, described as introducing strict penalties to curb polygamous practices. Its stated objective is to eliminate such practices in the state. The Bill applies to residents of Assam. It addresses marriages that were formed before the law came into force, and it includes provisions for women who were affected by polygamous marriages. Existing Indian law already treats the issue in different ways. Some statutes prohibit bigamy for certain communities, while the personal laws of other communities allow multiple marriages within limits. The Bill therefore sits at the meeting point of criminal law, family law and personal laws, and its design reflects the need to balance social reform with the rights of communities and individuals. Any such law must also be read alongside Fundamental Rights, because a marriage that violates them can be legally challenged under some personal laws. Debates on the subject often return to the same question, namely how far a single legal framework can respect the diversity of religious communities across the country.

quizzes.title: UCC and courts: short answers
quizzes.passage: A Uniform Civil Code would mean one common set of personal laws that applies to all citizens, irrespective of their religious affiliation. The framers of the Constitution did not intend total uniformity in this area. The Central Government favours a common code, calling different matrimonial laws for various religions a threat to the nation's unity. The 2018 Law Commission report suggested reforming and codifying family laws across religions instead of pursuing a UCC at this stage. The Supreme Court has also referred to the matter in several judgments. In the Shah Bano case, the Court highlighted the need for uniformity in personal laws. Later rulings on talaq-e-biddat, also called triple talaq, dealt with a practice within personal law. The Court has also praised one Indian state that has a functioning UCC, calling it an example for others. The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 also contains an offence for marrying again during the lifetime of a spouse, which is punishable with imprisonment and a fine. Personal laws continue to differ across religions in matters of marriage and property, and this difference is the core of the debate. Together these strands show how the UCC debate connects constitutional text, legislative reform and judicial rulings.

quizzes.title: Why the rupee weakened in 2025
quizzes.passage: The Indian rupee depreciated by over 5% in 2025 and, by December, had crossed 90 per US dollar. The fall was not the result of one sudden shock. Analysts instead pointed to a mix of global and domestic pressures that had been building over time. Strength in the US dollar was a major backdrop, and the rupee was also hit by delays in a trade arrangement between India and the United States that investors had been anticipating. Money flowed out of Indian markets as global risk sentiment shifted. On the domestic side, the gap between what India buys from abroad and what it sells drew close attention. Crude oil prices rose, and some exports to major destinations were under strain. Demand for dollars also grew in the currency market as businesses and traders responded to the expectation of further weakness in the rupee. The 90 level drew particular attention from traders, who treat such round-number thresholds as important. Market participants said the fall had built up over time rather than arriving in a single day. Experts said the rupee's path in the months ahead would depend on global financial conditions, external trade developments and domestic economic indicators.

quizzes.title: Ways to steady the rupee
quizzes.passage: When the rupee faces sustained pressure, policymakers can work on several fronts at once. One approach is to reduce how much India's trade depends on the dollar, so that more transactions with partner countries are settled in the domestic currency. A second approach is to make the rupee easier to trade and hold outside India, which would widen its use in global markets. Strengthening the external sector is another route, and this includes maintaining healthy foreign exchange reserves. The central bank can also step into the currency market, selling or buying dollars as conditions require, and it can adjust interest rates. Over the longer term, attention turns to structural matters. Improving export competitiveness, attracting foreign direct investment through better infrastructure and regulation, and making it easier to do business are all part of this picture. Gold imports also weigh on the external balance, so reducing them is part of the broader effort. Policy choices are also shaped by the need to control inflation. Taken together, these steps aim to ease pressure on the currency gradually, rather than resolving it in a single move.

quizzes.title: Repo Cut and Goldilocks: MCQ Practice
quizzes.passage: In December 2025, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) cut the policy repo rate to 5.25 per cent. The move was intended to sustain what the RBI called a Goldilocks phase, a balanced condition that is neither too hot nor too cold. In such a phase, the economy grows strongly while inflation stays low. Monetary policy works through the repo rate in both directions. When inflation rises, the central bank can make borrowing costly, which curbs excessive spending and slows investment. When the economy needs more money, the central bank lowers the rate, so that loans become cheaper for banks, which then pass lower interest rates on to borrowers and businesses. The December cut was justified on three grounds. Inflation had fallen sharply below the lower end of the target range, which created room for easing without risking price instability. Growth also remained robust despite global uncertainties. Finally, global trade headwinds and other external pressures made a pre-emptive stimulus useful in offsetting a slowing expansion. Lower rates are expected to boost lending, consumption and investment. They may, however, weaken the rupee and reduce returns on fixed deposits, which could discourage household savings. The rate decision itself is taken by a statutory body called the Monetary Policy Committee, which works within India's flexible inflation-targeting framework.

quizzes.title: MPC and Inflation Targeting: Typed Answer
quizzes.passage: India's monetary policy is framed within an inflation-targeting system. The Reserve Bank of India manages the money supply to achieve economic growth, which is different from fiscal policy handled by the Ministry of Finance. A statutory committee within the RBI decides the benchmark policy rate needed to keep inflation within a targeted range. The Central Government is empowered to constitute this committee, and its decisions are taken by majority vote. The Governor chairs it ex officio, and its decisions are binding on banks. India moved to flexible inflation targeting after an earlier expert panel formally set the target and its band. The inflation target is set by the government in consultation with the RBI. The RBI also releases a periodic report that explains the sources of inflation and its forecasts.

quizzes.title: Summit economics and payments
quizzes.passage:
India and Russia used their 23rd Annual Summit in New Delhi to widen cooperation well beyond their traditional areas. The summit came after the two countries upgraded their ties to a special and privileged strategic partnership, and it marked 25 years of that relationship. The leaders adopted a comprehensive programme meant to diversify bilateral ties beyond defence and energy. Its work is coordinated by a commission that handles trade, economic, scientific, technical and cultural cooperation between the two governments, and that body serves as the apex forum for economic dialogue between them.

Trade and finance formed a central part of the discussions. Both sides agreed to boost settlements in national currencies, and they decided to work on interoperability of their payment systems and digital currencies. Officials described this as a way to reduce reliance on Western financial channels. The leaders also reaffirmed their commitment to energy security, with continued support for nuclear power projects in India, including small modular reactors and future civil nuclear work.

The summit also addressed terrorism. Both countries called for strict action against all UN-listed terrorist organisations and endorsed a zero-tolerance approach grounded in international law. Connectivity and mobility were additional priorities, as the two governments pursued new routes for cargo and skilled professionals.

quizzes.title: Defence and logistics facts
quizzes.passage:
Defence cooperation remains one of the strongest pillars of India's partnership with Russia. The two countries have agreed on a reciprocal logistics arrangement that allows their armed forces to draw mutual support while operating away from home bases. Under this arrangement, each side can access the other's military facilities, ports and airspace, and it provides simplified refuelling and maintenance for deployments.

A high-level dialogue that brings together the foreign and defence ministers of both countries helps align their strategic priorities. Russia has long been among India's largest suppliers of defence equipment, and the two sides continue to pursue joint research, co-production under Make in India and transfer of military technology. Regular joint exercises between the armed forces add to this cooperation, and recent frigates have been commissioned into the Indian Navy.

Several major platforms reflect this partnership. A cruise missile is being developed jointly by an Indian research organisation and a Russian design bureau, while Indian production lines build multi-role fighter aircraft and main battle tanks based on Russian designs. India has also procured a long-range surface-to-air missile system from Russia, and a former Russian aircraft carrier has been refurbished for the Indian Navy.

quizzes.title: The Durand Line Border
quizzes.passage: The Durand Line is a long international boundary that separates Pakistan from Afghanistan. Its origins lie in the colonial period, when British India and Afghanistan were locked in a long and often violent relationship. Britain fought several wars with Afghanistan, and some of these conflicts ended in settlements that changed how Afghanistan's external relations were handled. The boundary itself was fixed through a late nineteenth-century arrangement that involved British officials and the Afghan ruler of the time. Its path crosses demanding terrain, from mountain ranges in the north to deserts further south. When British rule over the subcontinent ended, the boundary passed to Pakistan, while Afghanistan has continued to question its legitimacy. Many communities that live near the line share ethnic and cultural ties across it, so the boundary affects families and tribes as well as governments. Tensions along the frontier have periodically resurfaced, and recent allegations of airstrikes near the line have drawn fresh attention to a dispute that began more than a century ago. Students preparing for current affairs should understand both the historical background and the modern implications of this boundary, since disputes of this kind shape regional security and diplomacy. Diplomatic exchanges about the border have often focused on whether the boundary is legitimate, and these debates continue to shape relations between the neighbouring states.

quizzes.title: Finance, Bonds and Cess

Indian entities have also long used rupee-denominated debt sold in overseas markets to attract foreign investment and reduce their dependence on domestic borrowing. On the revenue side, the government raises money through taxes, cesses and surcharges, and each is governed differently. A cess is levied for a specific purpose and used only for that purpose, while a surcharge adds to the Union's revenue without any specific earmarking. A new cess bill has also been proposed for goods that carry high health costs. Together, these measures show how the state balances revenue needs, public welfare and investor confidence in a changing economy. quizzes.title: Ecological Services of the Range: MCQ

Its landforms affect how air moves across north-western and northern India, and this in turn influences the climate of areas far from the hills. Its land also has a role in the water cycle, because rain that falls on the range can move into the ground. The forested stretches of the range are relevant to the National Capital Region, where they contribute to the quality of the air. The hills are home to a wide variety of living things, and plants, birds and animals find habitat across the range. The surrounding landscape also includes wildlife sanctuaries and bird parks, reflecting this biological richness. The range is also a source of several important rivers, which links its ecology to water supplies across the region. The range stretches across Gujarat, Rajasthan, Haryana and Delhi, so these effects are felt across several states. Taken together, these functions connect the hills to the climate, water, air and biodiversity of the plains beside them. The hills also host a variety of birds and other animals, which adds to their biological importance across the region.

quizzes.title: Case for Replacing MGNREGA

quizzes.title: Personal laws and marriage
quizzes.passage: Marriage in India is governed by personal laws that differ according to religion, so the legal position on a second marriage is not the same for every community. Statutes differ on whether a second marriage during the subsistence of the first is treated as wrongful, while other personal laws leave room for more than one spouse. Criminal law also addresses marrying again during the lifetime of a spouse, under a code enacted in 2023. The Bill applies to residents of Assam and also covers individuals engaged in polygamous marriages outside the state, which gives it a reach beyond the state's own population. The Uniform Civil Code is the idea of a common set of personal laws that would apply to all citizens irrespective of religious affiliations. Several judgments of the Supreme Court have discussed the need for reform of personal laws over the decades. The Law Commission has also examined the subject in its consultation report. The Bill's objective is to eliminate polygamous practices across India, not only in Assam. The debate on uniformity has continued for many decades. quizzes.title: Who Gains and Who Pays
quizzes.passage: A currency's fall against foreign currencies has effects that run in more than one direction through an economy. Some effects are favourable, while others add costs to households, businesses and the government. The booklet presents these consequences under two headings, positive and negative, which helps readers weigh gains against burdens. Trade, government budgets and companies are all touched by such changes, and the effects can be felt in different ways by different groups. In 2025 the rupee's weakness drew close attention in financial markets, even though India's economy showed strong growth at the time. The booklet also discusses measures aimed at stabilising the rupee. The booklet's account therefore covers both sides of the picture, so readers can see how each consequence is grouped under its heading and how the two headings relate to one another in the economy section. Under the positive heading, the booklet lists effects that make some parts of the economy more competitive. Under the negative heading, it lists effects that raise costs for households, businesses and the government. The booklet also explains the reasons behind several of these effects, so each one can be understood in context rather than in isolation. The rupee's path in 2025 is one example of how such effects appear in practice, since its weakness was discussed alongside India's growth.

quizzes.title: Repo Rate and Other Tools
quizzes.passage: Monetary policy is formed and managed by the central bank to control a nation's overall money supply and to achieve economic growth. It differs from fiscal policy, which is managed by the Ministry of Finance and measures spending and taxation in the economy. The Reserve Bank of India releases a Monetary Policy Report once every six months, explaining the sources of inflation and forecasting it for six to eighteen months ahead. The Monetary Policy Committee is chaired by the RBI Governor and determines the policy rate required to achieve the inflation target. The repo rate is the central tool in this framework. When inflation is high, the central bank raises it so that the flow of money in the economy slows down. Borrowing becomes expensive for businesses and industries, investment slows, and excessive spending is curbed. Changes in this rate pass through to the cost of credit across the economy, so lenders and borrowers both feel the effect. The central bank also has other instruments at its disposal. Each of them acts on a different part of the banking system, and each is designed for a specific purpose. Together these tools let the central bank steer liquidity, price stability and growth in the economy, which is the broad aim of monetary policy.

Apart from the repo rate, the central bank has several other instruments, and each of them acts on a different part of the banking system. The central bank uses these tools together to balance liquidity, price stability and growth, which are the goals of monetary policy. quizzes.title: Price Indices and Their Coverage
quizzes.passage: Prices in an economy do not all move together, so official statisticians rely on several indices to track them. Each index is built with its own scope and method. One widely used measure groups household spending into commodity groups such as food, fuel and light, clothing and footwear, housing, pan, tobacco and intoxicants, and miscellaneous items. The same kind of measure also appears in separate versions for agricultural labourers, rural labourers and industrial workers. Each commodity group carries a weight, expressed as a percentage, that determines how much it influences the final figure. A group with a higher weight therefore matters more to the index. The choice of index changes what a number means, so readers must check what each one covers before comparing figures. Some measures capture a broad range of spending, while others rely on a narrower set of items. Two sources that track the same period can therefore show different movements, even when both are official. Knowing what each series includes is the starting point for reading any published price figure. Index values are compared with a reference point, and the coverage of each measure determines which prices enter that comparison. Some measures are built on a narrow set of commodities, while others are compiled from a much wider set of items.

quizzes.title: Price Indices and Their Coverage
quizzes.passage: Price movements in an economy are followed through statistical indices rather than through a single figure. An index tracks a set of goods and services over time and compares their prices with those in a chosen base period. Each item in the set is given a weight, usually expressed as a percentage, which shows how much that item contributes to the final number. Because the set of items and the weights differ from one index to another, the same economy can present different figures depending on the index used. One index breaks household spending into groups such as food, fuel and light, clothing and footwear, housing, and miscellaneous items, each with its own percentage weight. The publishing body and the method note therefore matter as much as the headline value. A reader who wishes to compare two numbers should first check which goods and services each index includes, whether the index covers services, and which period is treated as the reference. Changes measured from the base period are read as movements in the index, and a rise or fall in the value shows how the set of items has moved. Careful readers therefore look at coverage, weights and reference period together before deciding what a change in an index means.

quizzes.title: Origins and Functions of the RBI
quizzes.passage: The Reserve Bank of India is the institution that the country relies on for managing its financial system. Its role has grown over time, and it now touches the government, the banking sector and the wider public. The Bank sets policy and keeps watch over the institutions that carry it out. Among its responsibilities it holds and manages the foreign exchange reserves that the country maintains. The Bank was created after a period of official consideration, under a law passed when the country was under foreign rule. Its work is defined by statute, and that statute gives it powers over money and banking. Monetary policy, which the Bank manages, differs from fiscal policy handled by the Ministry of Finance, which deals with government spending and taxation. The Bank publishes a Monetary Policy Report once every six months to explain the sources of inflation. The RBI Governor is the ex-officio chairperson of the Monetary Policy Committee, which determines the policy rate needed to meet the inflation target. The Bank's influence on everyday finance is therefore broad, and its statute defines the scope of its authority. The Bank's presence is felt in everyday finance, through the notes people carry, the rates banks charge and the rules that govern the wider system.

quizzes.title: Origins and Functions of the RBI
quizzes.passage: The Reserve Bank of India sits at the centre of the country's financial system. The institution was not always under public control, since it began with private stakeholders before the state took over. It was set up under a law passed by the British government and began operating in an eastern city, on a fixed day of the year. Its tasks are varied. It grants bank licences, approves the opening of branches and inspects banks. In the foreign exchange area it holds the country's reserves, manages its dealings and enforces exchange rules. It also manages the financial affairs of the central government and provides advances to state governments through agreements. The Bank acts as a banker to other banks and to the government. Monetary policy, which the Bank manages, differs from fiscal policy handled by the Ministry of Finance. The Bank also publishes a Monetary Policy Report and intervenes to limit volatility in the rupee against the dollar. Its functions are set out in the RBI Act of 1934, and that Act sets the framework within which the Bank works with the government, the banking sector and the public. The Bank's tasks are discharged across its offices and departments in the country. Together these roles make the Bank a central point of the country's money and banking system.

quizzes.title: Corridors and Connectivity with Russia
quizzes.passage:
India and Russia treat transport links as a practical part of their wider partnership. The 23rd Annual Summit, held in New Delhi, discussed several corridors that could make the movement of goods between the two countries easier. The most prominent proposal is the Chennai-Vladivostok Maritime Corridor, a sea route linking the Indian port of Chennai with the Russian port of Vladivostok. Its stated purpose is to carry cargo and reduce the time needed to reach Russia compared with the existing route between the two ports.

A second channel is the International North-South Transport Corridor, a transport network that includes India, Russia and other member states. Both corridors appear in the summit's connectivity agenda, which also covers Russia's Far East and the Arctic.

Cooperation in the Far East and the Arctic is guided by a separate programme, which lists several sectors for joint work. These sectors include mining, pharmaceuticals and manpower. The summit also addressed trade more generally, with a comprehensive programme meant to diversify ties beyond defence and energy.

The partnership itself has a long history. India and Russia have a treaty of peace and friendship, and in 2010 their relationship was upgraded to a Special and Privileged Strategic Partnership. Transport planning sits alongside these political agreements, and the summit documents list connectivity among its major outcomes.

The meeting marked 25 years of strategic partnership, and its outcomes covered economic, defence, energy and migration topics. The summit also marked Russia's President's first visit to India in four years.

Security was another focus of the discussions. Both sides condemned attacks that had taken place in their countries. The two governments also discussed their cooperation in international forums such as the UN, G20, BRICS and SCO.

Honours also featured in the summit's record. Russia's highest national award was conferred on Prime Minister Narendra Modi for his contribution to fostering India-Russia ties. The award was presented during the visit, and it recognised the work done to strengthen bilateral relations.

Dialogue between the two countries also takes other forms. A platform for enhancing the Special and Privileged Strategic Partnership, which was upgraded in 2010, involves government bodies and research institutions. The summit documents describe cooperation in areas such as nuclear energy and defence, and they mention regular defence exercises as well. Security was another focus of the discussions. Both sides condemned attacks that had taken place in their countries. The two governments also discussed their cooperation in international forums such as the UN, G20, BRICS and SCO.

Honours also featured in the summit's record. Russia's highest national award was conferred on Prime Minister Narendra Modi for his contribution to fostering India-Russia ties. The award was presented during the visit, and it recognised the work done to strengthen bilateral relations.

Dialogue between the two countries also takes other forms. A platform for enhancing the Special and Privileged Strategic Partnership, which was upgraded in 2010, involves government bodies and research institutions. The summit documents describe cooperation in areas such as nuclear energy and defence, and they mention regular defence exercises as well. The defence agenda also includes joint research and development, co-production under Make in India, and military technology transfer.

quizzes.title: Karbi Anglong and Workplace Rights
quizzes.passage:
Unrest in Karbi Anglong, the largest district of Assam, has renewed debate on land and resource rights. The current instability began with a hunger strike by indigenous tribal groups, who demanded the eviction of long-settled non-tribal communities. Protesters argue that these settlements in protected grazing and tribal lands are unconstitutional and illegal. The district is administered by an autonomous council that works under a constitutional scheme giving autonomy to tribal areas in the North-East. A tripartite peace accord signed in 2021 aimed to end decades of insurgency and promised the council greater legislative, executive and administrative powers.

Workplace rights are also under debate. A private member's bill introduced in the Lok Sabha seeks to give employees a statutory right to refuse work calls, emails or messages beyond working hours and on holidays. Such bills are introduced by MPs who are not ministers, and their passage is uncommon. Constant digital availability is linked to anxiety, sleep-related disorders and burnout.

Harassment complaints form another part of this debate. A Supreme Court judgment held that a woman can approach the Internal Complaints Committee at her own workplace when the harasser is an outsider. The ruling expands the jurisdiction of the law on sexual harassment at work, which is based on guidelines issued by the Supreme Court. Its aim is to prevent, prohibit and redress harassment, and it applies to all women irrespective of employment status.
